assistant_reasoning: Section 825.104(a): an employer is covered if it employs 50 or more employees for each working day during each of 20 or more calendar workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year. 200 employees is well above 50 and there is no fact suggesting any of the workweek conditions are unmet. Covered.

The test is not peak headcount. It requires 50 or more employees on each working day of each of 20 or more workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year. The company hit 60 in only a single week; every other day of the past two years it had 8 employees. One qualifying week is far short of 20. Not covered.
48 employees, sustained, is still below the 50-employee threshold. Not covered.

Section 825.105(c) provides that employees on leave are counted where there is a reasonable expectation of return, but a laid-off employee with no employer/employee relationship is not counted. These 12 are laid off with no expectation of return, so they are excluded: 60 - 12 = 48. This is below the 50-employee threshold.

Section 825.105(b) is explicit: anyone on the payroll is considered employed each working day and must be counted whether or not any compensation is received for the week. The unpaid weeks are a payroll processing delay, so the three-week gap does not remove them. Counted.

The two sites are in different cities with separate supervisors and separate vehicles, so they are separate worksites rather than a single campus. Under the rule, workers whose worksite is New Jersey are not counted in determining eligibility of employees whose home base is the Ohio worksite. Not included.
For an employee whose home base is New Jersey, the converse of the rule applies: the Ohio workers are counted in determining that employee's eligibility. Included.

Section 825.111(a)(1) states that separate buildings in reasonable geographic proximity, used for the same purpose, and sharing the same staff and equipment are a single worksite. These two buildings are 900 feet apart, serve the same purpose, and share one shift supervisor and one fleet of vans. That is the single worksite case, so they aggregate to one worksite of 180 employees, not two of 90.

The size exemption is retrospective. Section 1904.1(b)(2) requires you to determine peak employment during the last calendar year, and (a)(1) exempts a company that had 10 or fewer employees at all times during that year. This company had 30 in March and April, so the condition fails. The low current headcount does not restore the exemption. Records are required.
10 or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year is exactly the stated exemption, and the company has met it continuously. Exempt from recordkeeping under 1904.1.

The industry exemption applies to individual business establishments, not to the company as a whole. Only establishment A is in a listed industry group; B and C are not, so B and C must keep records. A does not.
Both establishments are classified in listed industry groups, so each one independently qualifies for the partial industry exemption. Neither is required to keep records on that basis.
Section 1910.38(b) requires a written plan but expressly allows an employer with 10 or fewer employees to communicate the plan orally. 9 employees qualifies.

assistant_answer_note: The oral-communication allowance is limited to employers with 10 or fewer employees. This employer has 11, so the plan must be in writing.
